proved_step:
statement_start: For every n>=1, threshold t, variable order, and level k, the OBDD width of f(x)=[sum_i x_i >= t] at level k is at most k+1.
proof: Fix the first k variables in the chosen order. For any assignment a to them, let j(a) be its number of 1s. On the remaining variables y, the residual is f_a(y)=[j(a)+sum_i y_i>=t]=[sum_i y_i>=t-j(a)]. Hence residuals are determined by j(a) in {0,...,k}; there are at most k+1 distinct residual functions, which is exactly the OBDD width at level k.

statement_start: For every n>=1, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n<=W, integer threshold t, variable order, and level k, the OBDD width is at most kW+1.
statement: For every n>=1, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n<=W, integer threshold t, variable order, and level k in {0,...,n}, the Boolean threshold function f(x)=[sum_i w_i x_i >= t] has at most kW+1 distinct residual functions after fixing the first k variables in that order. Consequently its ordered binary decision diagram has size at most sum_{k=0}^n (kW+1)=W*n*(n+1)/2+n+1, hence polynomial size when W is polynomially bounded in n.
derivation: Fix a variable order and a level k. For any assignment alpha to the first k variables, let s(alpha) be the sum of w_i alpha_i over those variables. The residual on the remaining variables y is [sum_{i remaining} w_i y_i >= t-s(alpha)]. Since each fixed weight is an integer in [0,W], s(alpha) is an integer in [0,kW]. Thus there are at most kW+1 possible values of s(alpha), and assignments with the same value produce identical residual functions. The width at level k is therefore at most kW+1. Summing these width bounds over k=0,...,n gives the stated size bound. This argument covers zero weights and thresholds outside the attainable range as well.
